--- title: "Data structures and working with code" subtitle: "Session 2 · Topics 1.3 + 1.4 · Thu 3 Dec" format: revealjs --- ## Quick recap ::: {#d020f678 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} def bending_stress(F, t, L=150, b=40): """Max bending stress of a rectangular cantilever, MPa.""" return 6 * F * L / (b * t ** 2) for t in [10, 12, 14]: s = bending_stress(1500, t) print(f"t={t} mm: {s:.0f} MPa", "OK" if 355 / s >= 1.5 else "FAIL") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` t=10 mm: 338 MPa FAIL t=12 mm: 234 MPa OK t=14 mm: 172 MPa OK ``` ::: ::: ::: {.muted} Variables, types, `if`, `for`, functions. Today: how to keep **many** values together, and what to do when the code does not work. ::: ## Today ::: {.agenda} 1. Lists — ordered collections 2. Tuples — fixed records 3. Dictionaries — values by name 4. Sets — unique values 5. Reading error messages 6. Modules and `import` 7. Files: reading and writing text ::: # Lists {.divider} ## A list holds many values in order ::: {#4cc5b51e .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} thicknesses = [8, 10, 12, 16, 20] # mm print(len(thicknesses)) print(thicknesses[0], thicknesses[-1]) # first, last print(thicknesses[1:3]) # slice: index 1 and 2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 5 8 20 [10, 12] ``` ::: ::: - indexes start at **0**; negative indexes count from the end - slice `a[start:stop]` — `stop` is **not** included (like `range`) ## Changing a list ::: {#c9b3a2bf .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} loads = [500, 1000, 1500] loads.append(2000) # add at the end loads[0] = 750 # replace an item loads.remove(1000) # remove by value print(loads) print(sorted([3, 1, 2]), max(loads), min(loads), sum(loads)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [750, 1500, 2000] [1, 2, 3] 2000 750 4250 ``` ::: ::: - lists are **mutable** — you can change them after creating them - `sorted()`, `max()`, `min()`, `sum()`, `len()` work on any list of numbers ## Building a list in a loop ::: {#d1533c02 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} stresses = [] for t in thicknesses: stresses.append(bending_stress(1500, t)) print([round(s, 1) for s in stresses]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [527.3, 337.5, 234.4, 131.8, 84.4] ``` ::: ::: The same in one line — a **list comprehension**: ::: {#3d67ddd9 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} stresses = [bending_stress(1500, t) for t in thicknesses] ok = [t for t in thicknesses if 355 / bending_stress(1500, t) >= 1.5] print(ok) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [12, 16, 20] ``` ::: ::: ## Looping over two lists together ::: {#79f952f3 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} for t, s in zip(thicknesses, stresses): print(f"{t:>3} mm {s:7.1f} MPa") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 8 mm 527.3 MPa 10 mm 337.5 MPa 12 mm 234.4 MPa 16 mm 131.8 MPa 20 mm 84.4 MPa ``` ::: ::: ::: {#dab233fa .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} for i, t in enumerate(thicknesses): print(i, t) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 0 8 1 10 2 12 3 16 4 20 ``` ::: ::: - `zip(a, b)` — walk through two lists side by side - `enumerate(a)` — get the position and the value # Tuples and dictionaries {.divider} ## Tuples: fixed records ::: {#68a43e25 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} design = (12.0, 4.5, 1500) # thickness, fillet radius, load t, r, F = design # unpacking print(t, r, F) # design[0] = 14 -> TypeError: tuples cannot be changed ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 12.0 4.5 1500 ``` ::: ::: - like a list, but **immutable** — good for things that belong together and should not change - you already met them: a function returning `stress, deflection` returns a tuple ## Dictionaries: values by name ::: {#f510fbf3 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} steel = {"name": "S355", "yield_MPa": 355, "E_GPa": 210, "density": 7850} print(steel["yield_MPa"]) steel["E_GPa"] = 205 # change steel["weldable"] = True # add a new key print(steel.keys()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 355 dict_keys(['name', 'yield_MPa', 'E_GPa', 'density', 'weldable']) ``` ::: ::: - `{key: value, ...}` — look things up by **key**, not by position - keys are usually strings; values can be anything ## Dictionaries in practice ::: {#066e343d .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} yield_strength = {"S235": 235, "S355": 355, "S460": 460} for grade, fy in yield_strength.items(): sf = fy / bending_stress(1500, 12) print(f"{grade}: SF = {sf:.2f}") print(yield_strength.get("S690", "unknown grade")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` S235: SF = 1.00 S355: SF = 1.51 S460: SF = 1.96 unknown grade ``` ::: ::: - `.items()` gives key–value pairs - `.get(key, default)` avoids an error when the key is missing ## A calculation run as a dictionary {.smaller} ::: {#a3fb1949 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} run = {"run_id": "R001", "thickness_mm": 12, "load_N": 1500} run["stress_MPa"] = bending_stress(run["load_N"], run["thickness_mm"]) run ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ``` {'run_id': 'R001', 'thickness_mm': 12, 'load_N': 1500, 'stress_MPa': 234.375} ``` ::: ::: A list of such dictionaries = a **table**: ::: {#07842289 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} runs = [ {"run_id": "R001", "thickness_mm": 12, "load_N": 1500}, {"run_id": "R002", "thickness_mm": 10, "load_N": 2500}, ] for r in runs: print(r["run_id"], round(bending_stress(r["load_N"], r["thickness_mm"]), 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` R001 234.4 R002 562.5 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.tip} This is exactly the shape of the data in Module 2. pandas will make it much more comfortable. ::: ## Sets: unique values ::: {#ffb17105 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} materials_used = ["S355", "S235", "S355", "S355", "S460"] unique = set(materials_used) print(unique, len(unique)) print("S690" in unique) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` {'S235', 'S460', 'S355'} 3 False ``` ::: ::: - no duplicates, no order - fast `in` checks; useful for "which different values do I have?" ## Which structure when? | Structure | Syntax | Ordered | Changeable | Typical use | |---|---|---|---|---| | list | `[1, 2, 3]` | yes | yes | series of values | | tuple | `(1, 2, 3)` | yes | no | one fixed record | | dict | `{"a": 1}` | by insertion | yes | values by name | | set | `{1, 2, 3}` | no | yes | unique values | ## Your turn (8 min) ::: {.exercise} 1. Create a list of five `(thickness, load)` tuples of your choice. 2. For each, compute the stress and store the results in a **list of dictionaries** with keys `thickness_mm`, `load_N`, `stress_MPa`, `sf`. 3. Print only the runs with `sf < 1.5`. 4. With a dictionary of steel grades, find the cheapest grade (lowest yield) that makes every run pass. ::: # Working with code: errors {.divider} ## Errors are normal ::: {#1f7b4f54 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} loads = [500, 1000, 1500] print(loads[3]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
IndexError                                Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[14], line 2
      1 loads = [500, 1000, 1500]
----> 2 print(loads[3])

IndexError: list index out of range
``` ::: ::: ::: How to read a **traceback**: 1. go to the **last line**: the error type and message 2. look one line up: where it happened 3. ask: what value did Python have at that moment? ## The errors you will see most | Error | Usual reason | |---|---| | `SyntaxError` | missing `:`, bracket or quote | | `IndentationError` | wrong spaces at the start of a line | | `NameError` | a typo in a name, or the variable was never created (cell not run?) | | `TypeError` | wrong type, e.g. `"12" + 3` | | `IndexError` | list position that does not exist | | `KeyError` | dictionary key that does not exist | | `ZeroDivisionError` | dividing by zero | | `ValueError` | right type, wrong value, e.g. `float("abc")` | ## Debugging tools you already have {.smaller} ::: {#c727f110 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} def safety_factor(F, t): s = bending_stress(F, t) print("DEBUG stress =", s) # look inside return 355 / s safety_factor(1500, 12) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` DEBUG stress = 234.375 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ``` 1.5146666666666666 ``` ::: ::: - `print()` intermediate values; `type(x)` when in doubt - test with simple numbers you can check by hand - `assert` — stop if something is not as expected: ::: {#e3a097de .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} t = -12 assert t > 0, f"thickness must be positive, got {t}" ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
AssertionError                            Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[16], line 2
      1 t = -12
----> 2 assert t > 0, f"thickness must be positive, got {t}"

AssertionError: thickness must be positive, got -12
``` ::: ::: ::: ## Handling expected problems: `try` / `except` ::: {#261d701a .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} values = ["12.5", "13", "n/a", "11.8"] clean = [] for v in values: try: clean.append(float(v)) except ValueError: print(f"skipped bad value: {v!r}") print(clean) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` skipped bad value: 'n/a' [12.5, 13.0, 11.8] ``` ::: ::: ::: {.muted} Catch only errors you expect and know how to handle. Never hide all errors with a bare `except:`. ::: # Modules and files {.divider} ## `import`: use code written by others ::: {#d9e9d8cb .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} import math print(math.pi, math.sqrt(2), math.radians(30)) from math import sin, cos print(round(sin(math.pi / 6), 3)) import statistics as st print(st.mean([1.2, 1.5, 1.9]), st.stdev([1.2, 1.5, 1.9])) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 3.141592653589793 1.4142135623730951 0.5235987755982988 0.5 1.5333333333333332 0.3511884584284246 ``` ::: ::: - **standard library** — comes with Python (`math`, `statistics`, `pathlib`, `csv`, ...) - other packages (NumPy, pandas) are installed separately — Session 3 ## Your own module Save the functions in a file `bracket.py`: ```python # bracket.py def bending_stress(F, t, L=150, b=40): return 6 * F * L / (b * t ** 2) ``` Then, in a notebook or another script in the same folder: ```python from bracket import bending_stress bending_stress(1500, 12) ``` ::: {.tip} Once a formula is checked, put it in a module. Every notebook then uses the same, tested version. ::: ## Writing and reading a text file ::: {#acefad38 .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} with open("results.txt", "w") as f: for t in [10, 12, 14]: f.write(f"{t},{bending_stress(1500, t):.1f}\n") with open("results.txt") as f: for line in f: t, s = line.strip().split(",") print(float(t), float(s)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 10.0 337.5 12.0 234.4 14.0 172.2 ``` ::: ::: - `with open(...) as f:` closes the file automatically - `"w"` write (overwrites), `"a"` append, default `"r"` read - each line is a **string**: `.strip()`, `.split(",")`, then convert ## Good habits - meaningful names: `stress_MPa`, not `x2` - one function = one job; docstring with units - comments explain **why**, the code shows **what** - run the notebook top to bottom (*Runtime → Restart and run all*) before you trust it - style guide: PEP 8 — 4 spaces, `snake_case`, lines not too long ## Your turn (10 min) ::: {.exercise} 1. Write the five runs from the previous exercise to `runs.csv` (header line + one line per run). 2. Read the file back, convert the numbers and compute the mean stress with `statistics.mean`. 3. Add one broken line (`R099,abc,1500`) to the file and make your reader skip it with `try` / `except`, printing a warning. ::: ## Summary - **list** `[]` ordered, changeable · **tuple** `()` fixed · **dict** `{k: v}` by name · **set** unique - list comprehensions: `[f(x) for x in items if condition]` - read tracebacks from the bottom; most errors are typos or wrong types - `import` modules; put checked functions in your own `.py` file - files: `with open(...)`, lines are strings **Next session:** your own Python environment and version control with Git. ## Practice at home (~1 h) - finish the exercises - write `read_runs(path)` that returns a list of dictionaries from a CSV-like file - before next session: create a free account on **github.com**
